items.text: Correction: the irreducible case
Counterexample to "$X$ irreducible, $Z$ geometrically irreducible and non-empty, $Z\to X$ $\Rightarrow X$ geometrically irreducible":
X=\operatorname{Spec}\mathbb R[x,y]/(x^2+y^2),\quad Z=\operatorname{Spec}\mathbb R\to X\ (x,y\mapsto0);\qquad x^2+y^2=(x+iy)(x-iy)\ \text{over }\mathbb C
Correct statement. $k'$ separably closed, $X'_i$ the irreducible components of $X_{k'}$, $p\colon X_{k'}\to X$:
X_{ij}=p(X'_i\cap X'_j),\qquad \Sigma=\bigcup_{i\ne j}X_{ij}\subset X

$\Sigma$ is independent of $k'$ (take $k'$ a separable closure; $p$ is then closed), closed if the irreducible components of $X$ are locally finite, and nowhere dense (maximal points of $X'_i$ lie over maximal points of $X$, flatness).
$\Sigma$ = the points of $X$ lying on more than one geometric irreducible component. Above: $\Sigma=\{0\}$.
Theorem. $X$ irreducible, $Z$ geometrically irreducible, $f\colon Z\to X$ with $f(Z)\not\subset\Sigma$. Then $X$ is geometrically irreducible.
E.g. when $X$ is geometrically normal or geometrically regular (local rings of $X'$ are domains); enough that one point of $Z$ goes to a geometrically normal point.

Proof. $k_1/k$ finite Galois; show $X_1=X_{k_1}$ irreducible. $z\in Z$ with $f(z)\notin\Sigma$, $z_1$ above it; $T$ an irreducible component of $X_1$ containing $f_1(Z_1)$ — unique since $f_1(z_1)$ lies on only one component.
\gamma\in\Pi:\ \gamma(T)\supset\gamma f_1(Z_1)=f_1(Z_1)\ \Longrightarrow\ \gamma(T)=T
T=p^{-1}(p(T)),\quad p(T)\ \text{dense (flat) and closed (integral)}\ \Longrightarrow\ p(T)=X,\ T=X_1
Dictionary: étale $k$-schemes $\leftrightarrow$ $\Pi$-sets
X\ \longleftrightarrow\ E=X(\bar k)\quad(\text{discrete }\Pi\text{-set, continuous action})
$X$ connected non-empty $\iff$ $X\simeq\operatorname{Spec}K$, $K/k$ finite separable $\iff$ $\Pi$ acts transitively on $E\ne\varnothing$.
Connected components of $X$ $\leftrightarrow$ $\Pi$-orbits in $E$; $X$ quasi-compact $\iff$ $E$ finite.
Finite inverse limits and all direct limits correspond (and are computed in the category of all schemes over $k$; not so for infinite inverse limits).
Monomorphisms $\leftrightarrow$ injective maps; epimorphisms $\leftrightarrow$ surjective maps (also epimorphisms among all schemes, $=$ faithfully flat).
Torsors under a constant group
$G$ a discrete group acting on $X$ (étale), $G_k$ constant. $X$ is a $G_k$-torsor iff
G_k\times X\xrightarrow{\ (g,x)\mapsto(gx,x)\ }X\times X\ \text{isomorphism},\qquad X\to e\ \text{epimorphism}
In terms of $E$: $G$ acts on the right on $E$ commuting with $\Pi$; $E$ a $G$-torsor as a set.
Choosing an origin $a\in E$, $E\simeq G$; $\Pi$ acts by automorphisms of the torsor = left translations by elements of $G$:
\{\text{torsors under }G_k\text{ with a geometric point}\}\longleftrightarrow\operatorname{Hom}_{\text{cont}}(\Pi,G)
The torsor is connected iff $\Pi\to G$ is surjective: a Galois extension of $k$ with group $G$ $\leftrightarrow$ a surjection $\Pi\twoheadrightarrow G$.
The scheme $\underline{\pi}_0(X/k)$

$X_{k'}$ locally connected with components defined over a finite extension (e.g. $X$ quasi-compact): $X\to T=\underline\pi_0(X/k)$ is characterised by $T$ étale and the morphism has non-empty geometrically connected fibres; $T(\bar k)=\pi_0(X_{k'})$.
Underlying space of $T$ = the set of ordinary connected components of $X$ (discrete).
Local ring: for $t\in T$, $X_t$ the corresponding component:
\kappa(t)=\text{largest subalgebra of }\Gamma(X_t,\mathcal O_{X_t})\ \text{étale over }k
$\underline\pi_0$ commutes with products and base change:
\underline\pi_0(X\times_kY/k)=\underline\pi_0(X/k)\times_k\underline\pi_0(Y/k)
$G$ locally of finite type: $\underline\pi_0(G/k)$ is an étale group scheme, and
\underline\pi_0(G/k)=G/G^0
A non-finite-type example
$X=\operatorname{Spec}k'$, $k'$ a separable closure of $k$, $k'=\varinjlim k_i$ Galois, $\Pi_i=\operatorname{Gal}(k_i/k)$:
X_{k'}=\varprojlim X_{i,k'},\quad X_{i,k'}=\text{constant scheme }\Pi_i;\qquad |X_{k'}|=\varprojlim\Pi_i=\Pi\ \ (\text{compact, totally disconnected})

Structure sheaf: the locally constant $k'$-valued functions on $\Pi$. Connected components = points; $\pi_0(X_{k'})=\Pi$ as a profinite set: in general $\underline\pi_0$ is a pro-object, not a discrete set.
